title: Defences removed by the judge, not considered by the jury
subtitle: The system trusts jurors to judge the evidence, but gives judges control over the legal framework and the evidence they receive.
summary: Why can a judge rule out a defence before the jury hears it? Where does legal gatekeeping end and deciding the facts begin? A closer look at pre-trial rulings, criminal damage, reasonable excuse and jury independence.
scope: England and Wales · Crown Court jury trials. A defence can be ruled unavailable before or during trial—not only pre-trial. Removing a defence, excluding evidence and directing a verdict are different decisions.
status_note: Legislation, appellate judgments and official guidance are distinguished from our analysis and reform proposals. This is a study of the legal framework, not a finding that a defence was wrongly excluded in any particular ongoing prosecution.

highlights.label: Legal availability
highlights.detail: An unpopular or unlikely defence is not automatically an unavailable one.

highlights.label: Jury independence
highlights.detail: Wang protects the jury’s decision—even where the outcome seems obvious.

highlights.label: Accountability
highlights.detail: Reconsideration, limited early appeals and conviction appeals are distinct routes.

sections.title: Who decides what?
sections.intro: The jury has the verdict, but not unrestricted control over the questions it may decide.

table.caption: From defining an offence to reaching a verdict
rows: Parliament and, where applicable, common law
What conduct is criminal and what can justify or excuse it
Which evidence and arguments to put forward, subject to disclosure and procedural obligations
Admissibility and whether a proposed defence has a sufficient legal and evidential foundation
What facts are proved and whether applying the directed law establishes guilt

paragraphs.text: Wang explains that jurors find facts and apply the law as directed by the judge. The table is a simplified map of that division, not a claim that every issue fits neatly into a factual or legal box. Admissibility hearings can themselves require a judge to resolve factual disputes; that is different from taking over the jury’s decision on guilt.

The institutional case for this division is consistency, protection against unfair evidence, and reviewable legal rulings. The objection is equally important: controlling the inputs can shape the outcome. Jurors cannot assess evidence they never receive. Whether that control is justified depends on the particular legal rule, the evidence and the reasons given—not simply on calling the excluded material irrelevant.

sections.title: How does a defence reach—or fail to reach—the jury?
sections.intro: The infographic’s stages in accessible text. There is no single fixed day when every defence must be accepted or removed.

entries.title: 1. Identify the defence and the facts supporting it

paragraphs.text: A Crown Court defence statement must identify the nature of the defence, disputed facts and why they are disputed, facts relied upon, and points of law with supporting authorities. Merely naming a defence does not explain how its conditions could be met. The statement identifies the case to be advanced; it is not a judicial decision allowing or excluding that case.

CPS disclosure guidance gives the normal Crown Court deadline as 28 days after the prosecution complies, or purports to comply, with initial disclosure. The court can extend it. That deadline is for defence disclosure—not a universal deadline for a judge to rule on legal availability.

entries.title: 2. Resolve the legal question, before or during trial

paragraphs.text: Section 40 of the Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996 permits pre-trial rulings on admissibility and other legal questions, on a party’s application or the judge’s initiative. Legal argument is addressed to the judge, not decided by the jury. An ordinary pre-trial hearing must not be confused with the special statutory preparatory hearings that have their own appeal provisions.

At trial, the position may also depend on the evidence actually called. A ruling on a proposed legal defence is not the same as finding the defendant’s account untrue. The question is whether the issue can properly be put to the jury under the applicable law.

entries.title: 3. Test legal sufficiency—not the judge’s preferred verdict

paragraphs.text: There are two different problems: a defence may have no evidential foundation, or the material advanced may be incapable of supporting the required conclusion before a reasonable, properly directed jury. Neither is merely a prediction that the jury will probably reject it. Different defences have different ingredients and burdens; there is no single free-standing test of whether the defendant has a good moral reason.

The 2024 Attorney General’s Reference reaffirms the no-reasonable-jury threshold and requires considerable caution. The judge must not substitute their own decision for the jury’s. Taking an account at its highest is a useful way to identify a missing legal ingredient; it does not make every asserted belief legally sufficient.

If available, the defence can be considered with relevant, admissible evidence and appropriate jury directions. For criminal-damage lawful excuse, once sufficiently raised, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. That allocation should not be assumed for every defence under every statute.

If unavailable, the judge does not leave that legal route to acquittal to the jury. Evidence relevant only to that route may be excluded. The prosecution must still establish guilt; withdrawing a defence does not authorise a directed guilty verdict or eliminate other live issues.

sections.title: Wang: the safeguard cuts both ways
sections.intro: A judge may direct an acquittal where the prosecution case is insufficient. There is no equivalent power to direct a jury to convict.

entries.title: The jury cannot be reduced to a formality

paragraphs.text: The House of Lords quashed Wang’s conviction after the judge directed a guilty verdict. Paragraph 18 rejects any power to give that direction. The result was not conditional on whether an acquittal seemed likely: paragraph 17 says the defendant’s explanation could contain nuances that jurors, rather than the judge, should evaluate.

Paragraph 14 is particularly important. It accepts withdrawal where there truly is no evidence of lawful excuse, but criticises treating the tenuous connection in Hill and Hall as something the judge could conclusively decide instead of the jury. It also rejects the directions to convict. Reading Wang only as permission for judicial gatekeeping misses its warning against encroaching on the jury’s work.

Our analysis: the difficult boundary is not judge versus jury in the abstract. It is the difference between identifying a legally impossible defence and deciding a contestable inference that belongs to the jury. Later appellate decisions retain gatekeeping; Wang prevents it becoming a licence to determine guilt.

sections.title: Criminal damage: honest belief does not open every door
sections.intro: A sincere moral justification, a statutory lawful excuse and a human-rights argument are not interchangeable.

entries.title: Consent and protection of property are distinct routes

paragraphs.text: Section 5(2)(a) concerns belief in consent by someone believed entitled to give it, including belief that they would consent if they knew of the damage and its circumstances. Section 5(2)(b) concerns acts done to protect property or a property right or interest, with beliefs about immediate need and reasonable means. Section 5(3) makes honesty, not justification, decisive for the beliefs it addresses. Section 5 also has defined limits on the offences to which it applies.

These are not blanket permissions to damage property for an important cause. In particular, section 5(2)(b) is about protecting property, not a general defence of saving lives. Other recognised defences require their own analysis; section 5(5) preserves them rather than establishing that they succeed in any given case.

entries.title: The 2024 reference: which circumstances count?
entries.citation: Attorney General’s Reference No 1 of 2023 [2024] EWCA Crim 243

paragraphs.text: The court distinguished the fact that damage occurred as a protest from arguments about a cause’s merits or urgency. The latter did not count as the damage’s circumstances under section 5(2)(a). Belief in consent remained subjective, but its statutory subject matter was legally bounded. This is why an honest-belief defence can still face a legal threshold.

entries.title: The Colston reference did not overturn the acquittals
entries.kind: Court of Appeal judgment and statutory limit
entries.citation: Attorney General’s Reference No 1 of 2022 [2022] EWCA Crim 1259

paragraphs.text: The reference limited reliance on Convention proportionality for significant protest-related damage. It did not decide that the four acquitted defendants were guilty: other defences had been before the jury. Significant damage is not simply a synonym for the £5,000 trial-allocation boundary.

Section 36(7) of the Criminal Justice Act 1972 expressly prevents this reference procedure from affecting the original acquittal. Clarifying a rule for future cases and reversing a jury’s verdict are different powers. The same protection governs the 2024 reference; it is not an appeal against C’s acquittal.

sections.title: What does “not seen by the jury” actually mean?
sections.intro: A legal argument can disappear while some of the underlying evidence remains relevant for another reason.

entries.title: Unavailable defence, inadmissible evidence, and disputed facts

paragraphs.text: A defence-withdrawal ruling controls a route to acquittal. An admissibility ruling controls particular evidence. A jury’s factual finding concerns what the admitted evidence establishes. The decisions interact, but they are not identical: removing a defence does not automatically erase every fact associated with it. The relevance of each item to remaining issues must still be considered.

Nor is all exclusion directed against defendants. PACE section 78 permits exclusion of prosecution evidence where its admission would damage trial fairness to the specified degree, considering all the circumstances, including how it was obtained. It is a fairness safeguard, not a general statutory power to suppress the defence’s explanation.

entries.title: “Irrelevant” is a legal conclusion, not a description of importance
entries.kind: Official prosecution guidance and our analysis

paragraphs.text: CPS protest guidance explicitly tells prosecutors to resist irrelevant evidence when the proposed prevention-of-crime defence has no foundation. It distinguishes an imminent emergency from a wider political campaign and discusses remoteness in protection-of-property cases. This is the prosecution’s published guidance, not proof that every exclusion it seeks is correct.

Our criticism to test in an individual case: has the court explained why context cannot satisfy a specific legal requirement, or has it merely labelled the context unimportant? A moral or political issue can be profoundly important yet legally irrelevant to one defence. Conversely, a contested factual inference should not be relabelled a legal question just to remove it from the jury.

sections.title: Reasonable excuse: objective does not mean context-free
sections.intro: This connects directly with our section 58 research. It does not transplant the criminal-damage tests into terrorism legislation.

entries.title: The question cannot always be answered in the abstract
entries.citation: R v G; R v J [2009] UKHL 13

paragraphs.text: Paragraph 79 distinguishes an objectively reasonable excuse from an explanation the defendant personally regards as reasonable. Paragraph 81 requires attention to the actual circumstances and ordinarily leaves the assessment to the jury unless no reasonable jury could accept the excuse. Paragraph 83 refuses an abstract yes-or-no answer about curiosity without knowing what was done and why.

Our reading: objective assessment and contextual assessment can coexist. The threshold question asks whether this explanation could qualify under the law; the verdict question asks what the evidence establishes. Neither sincerity alone nor an abstract label such as curiosity settles both questions. The full paragraph 83 and wider case analysis are on the linked section 58 page.

sections.title: Does jury independence mean a right to disregard the law?
sections.intro: Protecting the jury’s verdict is not the same as authorising unrestricted decisions on which laws or defences should exist.

entries.title: Webster: the difference between a verdict and juror misconduct
entries.citation: R v Webster and others [2026] EWCA Crim 9

paragraphs.text: In a later criminal-damage appeal, the court considered directions prompted by jury-equity posters and placards. It rejected the argument that the jury had been threatened with imprisonment for acquitting, assessed the directions in the context of the whole trial, and dismissed the appeals. It described parts of the judge’s comments about the posters as more questionable, while finding the convictions safe.

Paragraph 73 distinguishes prohibited juror conduct concerning how someone intends to try the issue from the delivery of the verdict itself. Our conclusion is narrower than either slogan: no directed conviction does not create a general entitlement for advocates to invite jurors to ignore the law; nor should warnings about juror misconduct be described as punishment for returning not guilty.

sections.title: Can the ruling be challenged?
sections.intro: There is no general automatic interlocutory appeal against every adverse pre-trial decision.

paragraphs.text: A section 40 ruling is binding, but the judge can discharge or vary it in the interests of justice. Section 40(5) adds an important limit missing from the short infographic: a party cannot make that application unless there has been a material change of circumstances since the ruling or the last application. The statute also permits the judge to act on their own initiative.

Section 35 provides an appeal, with leave of the judge or Court of Appeal, from specified rulings under section 31(3) at formal preparatory hearings. It does not convert an ordinary section 40 ruling into an immediately appealable decision. Identifying the statutory hearing and ruling is essential before claiming an early appeal is available.

entries.title: After conviction: safety, not simply disagreement

paragraphs.text: An application for permission to appeal conviction is normally due within 28 days of conviction, even if sentence comes later. GOV.UK explains that a late application needs reasons and may receive an extension. An alleged error in withdrawing a defence can be raised, but the statutory question is whether the conviction is unsafe—not whether the appeal court would have managed the trial differently.

Allowing a conviction appeal results in quashing the conviction. A retrial may sometimes be ordered, so quashing does not invariably mean the proceedings are finished. A general discussion cannot establish whether a particular defendant has a viable ground without the ruling, evidence, directions and procedural record.

sections.title: Should more of this be for the jury?
sections.intro: That is a legitimate reform question. It should be separated from what the current law permits.

entries.title: More context—or power to recognise new justifications?
entries.kind: Independent Tribunal analysis · reform proposals, not existing rights

paragraphs.text: One reform would let jurors hear more context while retaining judicial directions about recognised defences. A much larger reform would let juries decide which justifications the law should recognise. The first changes the information available for a verdict; the second changes who determines criminal liability. They need different safeguards and cannot be treated as the same proposal.

sources.locator: para 8; starting point for our analysis

paragraphs.text: A narrower transparency proposal is a structured ruling identifying the precise defence, the legal ingredient said to be absent, the supporting evidence considered, why it cannot meet the threshold, and what context remains admissible for other purposes. Publish an appropriately redacted version where lawful. This is our proposal for clearer accountability—not a claim that judges presently give no reasons, or that all rulings can lawfully be published.

sources.locator: s 40; starting point for proposed reform

entries.title: The question worth putting to policymakers

paragraphs.text: Where a defendant advances a sincerely held justification supported by evidence, under what circumstances should a judge prevent the jury from considering it—and what safeguards stop an assessment of legal sufficiency becoming a substitute for the jury’s assessment of the facts?

sources.locator: paras 14, 17–18; context for our policy question

paragraphs.text: The organising principle is divided power, not unrestricted jury judgment. The remaining question is where that division should sit, how transparently it is applied, and how an erroneous exclusion can be corrected. For any particular case, start with the actual ruling rather than inferring what happened from a verdict or a campaign summary.
